blocks.x: The rate path

According to the [Manitoba Public Utilities Board, Order 43/26](https://www.pubmanitoba.ca/v1/proceedings-decisions/orders/pubs/26-orders/43-26.pdf), the Manitoba Hydro rate increase path to 2028 looks like this:

[The 4.0% applied to nearly all customers](https://www.pubmanitoba.ca/v1/contact-us/media/pubs/2026-nr/nr-mh-gra-fiscal-2026-2028-march-19-2026-english.pdf). The 3.5% and 3.0% are what the Board calls general revenue increases, which average out across customer classes: it expects some classes, including residential, to pay about 3.8% and 3.3%, and the largest industrial classes about 1% less.

Exact percentages come from a later compliance order, and [the Board's list of orders](https://www.pubmanitoba.ca/v1/proceedings-decisions/orders/electricity-26.html) showed none as of November 5, 2026. Compounded, the headline figures come to roughly 10.9% on average over three years.

These are electric rates. For buildings heated electrically, or with significant electric loads, electricity costs will rise steadily. A building heated with natural gas sees them mainly on its non-heating electricity, because gas rates are set separately.
Why doors matter as Manitoba Hydro rates rise
The envelope also means walls, roofs and windows. Windows get most of the attention in energy discussions, but doors deserve a look too, and they are the focus here:
**Main entrances** open all day, and worn closers and weatherstripping can let cold air pour in.
**Service and back doors** can be old, uninsulated steel or wood with damaged seals.
**Overhead and loading doors** in commercial buildings can leak a lot of air, so have a door specialist check them.
**Suite and unit entry doors** in apartment buildings can affect corridor pressure and comfort. They are often part of the fire separation, so check requirements before replacing them.
In Winnipeg's climate, a door with a visible gap or worn seals can be a constant drain on the heating system, and a source of complaints from occupants nearby.
Our view: start with the openings people complain about

Energy audits are useful, but often the quickest guide is the people in the building. Staff and tenants know which doors are drafty, which ones frost over, and which ones do not close properly. Those are the doors to look at first.
Professional [exterior door installation](/services/windows-and-doors) can address several problems at once:
**Air sealing:** new frames, thresholds and weatherstripping can reduce drafts.
**Insulation:** modern insulated doors perform better than old uninsulated units.
**Security:** better hardware and stronger frames.
**Appearance:** a new entrance improves first impressions.
**Accessibility:** a chance to address thresholds and widths, though a wider opening can need a building permit.
Incentives

For larger projects that reduce energy use by at least 20%, [Efficiency Manitoba's Commercial Deep Energy Retrofit Program](https://efficiencymb.ca/business/deep-energy-retrofit/) offers up to $12,000 for energy modelling and a performance incentive of $2.25 to $6.00 per square foot. Applicants need approval before starting work.

Door replacement alone will not meet the deep retrofit rules, but Efficiency Manitoba's [Building Envelope Program](https://efficiencymb.ca/business/building-envelope/) offers incentives for efficient windows and for [doors with glazing](https://efficiencymb.ca/business/building-envelope/incentive-details/), so a door with no glass does not qualify. Your contractor must be registered with Efficiency Manitoba, so ask any contractor you are considering, and get approval before you buy or install.

For houses, our [window and door replacement guide](/blog/window-and-door-replacement-winnipeg) covers [Efficiency Manitoba's rebate of $100 per qualifying ENERGY STAR triple-pane window or door](https://efficiencymb.ca/my-home/windows-and-doors-rebate/). Apartments are not eligible. Owners should check current program details before planning, and our [commercial rebates guide](/blog/efficiency-manitoba-commercial-rebates) explains how the business programs work.
Practical steps before winter deepens
**Walk the building** and note doors with visible gaps, frost, damaged frames or failing closers.
**Fix quick items now:** weatherstripping and closer adjustments can help this winter.
**Plan replacements** for the worst doors. Many door installations can be done in cold weather with proper planning, though some exterior work is easier in milder conditions.
**Price doors and windows together** where both need work, so you can compare doing them at once.
Beyond energy

Rising Hydro rates are a good reason to act, but door upgrades can pay off in other ways: more comfortable tenants and staff, better security, better-looking entrances, and less water and snow getting in.
How to estimate the payback

For owners who want numbers before committing, a simple approach helps. Start with the building's annual heating cost. Estimate the share lost through doors, based on an energy audit or on the number, condition and use of exterior doors.
If the building heats with electricity, apply the Hydro increases for your customer class to project that cost forward. Then compare the projected savings with the cost of replacement.

For most buildings, energy savings alone will not justify replacing every door. But for the worst-performing doors, especially high-traffic entrances, savings combined with comfort, security and reduced maintenance can make a strong case.
Don't forget the frame and threshold

Replacing a door slab without addressing the frame and threshold can leave the main source of leakage in place. Rotted or bent frames, gaps between the frame and the wall, and worn thresholds let air and water in regardless of how good the door is.

A complete installation includes the frame, proper insulation and sealing between the frame and the wall, a new threshold and properly adjusted hardware. That is what turns a new door into a real improvement in comfort and energy use.
The bottom line

With Manitoba Hydro's electricity revenue increases running every year to 2028, air leakage in electrically heated buildings is becoming more expensive. Exterior door installation is a straightforward way to seal the envelope, improve comfort and security, and limit the impact of rising energy costs.
